title: For All Teachers of Socratic Seminars
author: Andrew Ellison
summary: Andrew Ellison, a longtime Great Hearts leader, argues that struggling Humane Letters seminars are often held back not by poor questions, weak students, or hard texts but by mundane physical conditions hiding in plain sight. Borrowing Flannery O'Connor's point that fiction depends on concrete details like 'slippers on clerks,' he walks through seven such details. Tables must form a contiguous rectangle with no gaps, especially around the teacher, so the seminar reads as a unified community with the teacher as first among equals. Tables should be cleared of clutter, students must sit upright and close as at a dinner, and books must stay open with pencils in hand to anchor talk in the text. Breaks should follow the discussion's natural rhythm rather than the bell, formats should vary through close reading, student-generated questions, reading aloud, and board outlining, and teachers must actively coach students to speak up rather than mirroring soft voices. His closing move is to insist that these bodily and material conditions are necessary, if not sufficient, for the intellectual life of a seminar.
points: Any break in a contiguous table rectangle, such as a teacher sitting apart or empty seats near the leader, silently undermines the seminar's collective character.
Posture is both a sign and a cause of disengagement, so students should sit at seminar as they would at a dinner table, upright with hands visible.
Books must stay open and pens in hand throughout, keeping comments tethered to specific passages instead of drifting into generalities.
Breaking mechanically at the bell fragments a two-period course that should be planned as a unity, with some days devoted entirely to seminar.
A soft-spoken teacher tends to lower students' volume, so the teacher must act as the 'linguistic dynamo' and coach clear, audible speech.
quotes: In my experience, high school Humane Letters teachers who are struggling to make their seminar discussions lively and sustained often think that the problems lie in the precise phrasing of their discussion questions, in the students’ intellectual abilities, or in the difficulty of the texts themselves. But not infrequently, a large number of much smaller and mundane things are piled up in plain sight around the classroom, figuratively and literally, if not choking then at least restricting the airways of good Socratic discussion.

In these and other not-quite-right table formations, the contiguousness is interrupted in a way that undermines the unity and collective nature of the seminar. If the teacher is seated away from the students, the message is silently conveyed that he is the sage and center of attention rather than the first among equals.

Students are generally prone to bring far too much STUFF to class, piling up thick binders, folders, textbooks for other courses, pencil pouches, notebooks, and sundry objects. The Humane Letters seminar should be a two-hour exercise in de-cluttering. Nothing should be brought to class that isn’t needed, and the only things that should be on the table in front of each student are a text, a writing instrument, and (optionally) a notebook or notepad for those inclined to write notes.

When I visit a seminar class, I can tell at a glance that certain students are unengaged and will remain that way for all two hours if let be: the ones who sit back two feet from the table, arms folded, leaning back at a 45-degree angle, legs extended and feet flat on the floor. This physical posture is both a sign of and a contributing cause of mental torpor.

These various activities should be thought of as being split up not 50-50 each day, but divided over a series of days, some of which are devoted entirely to seminar, and others to non-seminar activities. Breaking on the bell is artificial, kills the day’s momentum, and leads to further fragmentation.

Note that all seven of these items are physical, not mental. They have not to do with the intellectual work of understanding complex and rich texts, but with the material and bodily conditions of the class.
